passage: The lights went out in the middle of the chemistry practical, and the lab fell into grey afternoon gloom. Jomon kept working by the window, counting drops carefully, and finished his titration first. His readings were neat, three trials within a whisker of each other. Mr Pillai walked past without looking at the sheet. Two minutes later Jomon knocked a stool with his foot. "Of course. Jomon again," Mr Pillai said. "Our naughty champion since Class 8." A few students laughed. Avni, at the next bench, leaned over. "Your numbers are better than mine," she whispered. Jomon shrugged and turned the sheet face down. On the bus home he didn't open his notebook at all. What was the point of trying, he thought, if only the stool got noticed?

qa.q: What did Mr Pillai say when Jomon knocked a stool?
qa.a: Mr Pillai said, 'Of course. Jomon again,' and called him 'our naughty champion since Class 8.'

qa.q: What is Jomon thinking on the bus home?
qa.a: Jomon feels discouraged and unseen, wondering what the point of trying is if only the stool gets noticed. 😔

qa.q: How could Mr Pillai handle the next practical better?
qa.a: He could look at every sheet before commenting and name Jomon's neat readings as clearly as he names his slips.

qa.q: How does Avni see Jomon's work compared with the teacher?
qa.a: Avni actually looks at his sheet and sees his numbers are better than hers, while Mr Pillai only noticed the stool.

grounding: A teacher's old 'naughty' label means a boy's careful practical goes unseen while one clumsy slip is called out.

passage: Amandeep had rewritten his Hindi essay twice, once at the dining table and once on the balcony of their Pune flat while the pressure cooker whistled. He handed it in on Monday, a day early. On Thursday the essays came back. Mrs Rao read three aloud and praised their opening lines. Amandeep's had a big tick and nothing else. Then, when his phone buzzed in his bag during the last period, she stopped the class. "Some people never change," she said, looking straight at him. "Trouble from day one." Chandrika turned around and mouthed, "Yours was good, I read it." Amandeep nodded, but his ears were hot. At home he pushed the essay into the back of a drawer without showing anyone.

qa.q: When did Amandeep hand in his Hindi essay?
qa.a: He handed it in on Monday, a day early.

qa.q: What do Amandeep's hot ears and hidden essay suggest he feels?
qa.a: They suggest he feels embarrassed and unseen, since his careful essay got only a tick while one buzzing phone drew a public comment.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do so his effort gets seen?
qa.a: He could show the essay to someone at home, or ask Mrs Rao privately for feedback on it, so the work is looked at apart from the label.

qa.q: What would change if Mrs Rao read Amandeep's essay without her old picture of him?
qa.a: She might notice the rewriting, praise it like the others, and treat the buzzing phone as a small slip rather than proof.

grounding: A teacher who sees a boy as 'trouble' skips his careful essay but spotlights a single slip in front of the class.

passage:
"Why the long face, Dhruv?" Manoj bhaiya asked, dropping onto the sofa.
"Sir put my name on the board again. For talking."
"Were you talking?"
"I asked Farhan for a ruler. One word. Half the class chatted all period and nothing happened to them."
"And the maths test? You said you got nineteen out of twenty."
"He handed it back without a word. Last week, when I got twelve, he said, 'Lazy boys get lazy marks.'"
Manoj bhaiya was quiet for a moment. "So he only sees the twelve."
"He decided in Class 8 that I'm the lazy one. Nothing I do changes it."
"Your nineteen is real, even if he skipped it."
Dhruv picked at a loose thread on the sofa. "Then why does it feel like it doesn't count?"

qa.q: What mark did Dhruv get in the maths test?
qa.a: Dhruv got nineteen out of twenty.

qa.q: Why does Dhruv feel his good mark doesn't count?
qa.a: Dhruv feels hopeless because Sir handed back the nineteen in silence but called him lazy over a twelve. The label seems to outweigh anything he does.

qa.q: What small step could Manoj suggest to help Dhruv?
qa.a: He could suggest Dhruv keep his marked work together and ask a parent or trusted teacher to raise the pattern calmly with Sir.

qa.q: How does Manoj bhaiya see the situation?
qa.a: Manoj bhaiya sees that the teacher only notices the twelve, and he reminds Dhruv that the nineteen is real anyway.

grounding: A teenage boy explains how a teacher's 'lazy' label makes his good marks go unnoticed while small slips are punished.

passage:
In Class 9, our maths teacher called me "the sleepy one" in the first week, because I yawned during the register. I'm Thomas, and that name followed me for a year.
When I finished a whole page of algebra, she said, "Someone must have helped the sleepy boy." When I forgot my compass once, the whole class heard about it. My friend Noor once swapped our notebooks as an experiment. Same answers, my handwriting copied by Noor. Noor's version got "Excellent." Mine, the week before, got "Late again?"
I stopped raising my hand. What was the point? It felt like she was only looking for the mistakes.
It changed in Class 10, with a new teacher who didn't know the name. By December I was answering again.

qa.q: What did the maths teacher call Thomas in the first week?
qa.a: She called him "the sleepy one".

qa.q: How did the label make Thomas feel, and what did it lead him to do?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and unfairly judged, as if his good work would never be noticed and she was only looking for mistakes, so he stopped raising his hand.

qa.q: What change turned things around for Thomas, and why did it help?
qa.a: A new teacher in Class 10 who didn't know the name judged his work fresh, so he felt seen again and started answering by December.

qa.q: How might Noor see the notebook experiment?
qa.a: Noor probably found it unfair and a little shocking that the same answers got 'Excellent' for Noor and 'Late again?' for Thomas, and may have wanted to prove it to Thomas.

grounding: A teenage boy labelled early as sleepy finds his good work ignored and small slips noticed, showing how a label limits what others see.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Ankita, St. Joseph's Higher Secondary, Wednesday.
Francis, Class 10, came in at lunch, not in trouble this time. He'd been sent twice last year for being "naughty" and I think that word has stayed on him. He showed me his science notebook: a full, neat experiment write-up with no remark at all. On the next page, one ink smudge, circled in red: "Careless as usual."
"Ma'am, I did the whole thing properly," he said quietly. "No one reads it. They just look for what I did wrong." He kept pressing his thumb into the notebook's edge.
I asked him what would help. He wanted one teacher to see his work without the old story attached.
What I did next: with Francis's permission, I spoke to his science teacher today. We agreed she would give feedback on his next two write-ups using his roll number only, without his name.

qa.q: What was circled in red on the next page of Francis's notebook?
qa.a: One ink smudge, circled in red: "Careless as usual."

qa.q: What does Francis pressing his thumb into the notebook edge suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt tense and let down, hurt that his proper work went unread while any small slip was picked out.

qa.q: What did Ankita do after listening, and why might it help?
qa.a: With his permission Ankita spoke to his science teacher, who agreed to mark his next two write-ups by roll number only, so his work could be judged without the old label.

qa.q: If you were the science teacher, what might you notice when marking by roll number?
qa.a: The teacher might discover that the neat, careful write-ups belong to Francis, and realise the 'naughty' label had been colouring what they saw.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenage boy whose earlier label means his good work is ignored while small slips are noticed.
